question: Fractional CRO vs full-time CRO for a Series A company?
body:
## Direct Answer

For most Series A companies, a **fractional CRO is the stronger first bet**: you get senior revenue leadership two to three days a week for roughly a quarter of a full-time package, which fits a $2M to $8M ARR business still proving repeatability. Hire a full-time CRO only once you have a working sales motion, several quota-carrying reps to manage, and a board mandate to scale hard — usually approaching Series B. The deciding factor is not seniority or budget alone but whether your bottleneck is *designing* the go-to-market engine or *operating* it at scale.

The choice between fractional and full-time chief revenue officer is one of the highest-leverage staffing decisions a Series A founder makes, and it is routinely made backwards. Founders over-index on the prestige of a full-time hire and under-index on burn, ramp risk, and organizational readiness. Below, we break down what each model actually delivers, when the crossover point arrives, how the economics compare on a fully loaded basis, and how to de-risk the decision whichever way you lean.

## What does a CRO actually own at Series A, and does that work need a full-time seat?

A CRO owns the entire revenue engine: sales, and usually some blend of marketing, customer success, revenue operations, and partnerships. At a mature company that is a sprawling operating job — forecasting to the board, managing multiple layers of managers, running deal desks, and defending a number every quarter. At Series A the same title covers a very different reality. The revenue "org" might be two account executives, an SDR, a part-time RevOps contractor, and the founder still closing the biggest deals. The work at this stage is disproportionately *design* work: defining the ideal customer profile, writing the first repeatable sales playbook, standing up a CRM that reflects a real pipeline, and instrumenting the metrics a Series B lead will diligence.

That distinction matters because design work is front-loaded and episodic, while operating work is continuous. A fractional CRO is built for the front-loaded phase — they parachute in, diagnose the funnel, architect the motion, hire the first real closers, and hand the operators a system to run. A full-time CRO is justified when the operating load becomes constant: daily deal coaching, weekly forecast calls, quarterly territory planning, and a team large enough that management itself is a full-day job. If your honest answer is "we need someone to *build the machine*," that is a fractional-shaped problem. If it is "we need someone to *run and scale a machine that already turns*," that leans full-time. For a deeper breakdown of how the revenue engine components fit together, see the [RevOps foundations primer](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-revops-foundations).

It also helps to separate the CRO role into the four jobs it quietly bundles: **architect** (design the ideal customer profile, pricing, and the motion), **recruiter** (hire and onboard the first quota-carriers), **coach** (raise the win rate of the people already selling), and **forecaster** (produce a number the board can trust). At Series A those four jobs are rarely all urgent at once. Most companies are acutely short on architect and recruiter capacity and only lightly loaded on coach and forecaster, because there are too few reps and too little pipeline history to forecast against. A fractional leader is optimized for the two jobs you actually need — architecture and recruiting — and can deliver the other two at low intensity. A full-time CRO is priced for a world where all four are simultaneously full-time, which is precisely the world you do not yet live in. Buying capacity you will not consume for another year is the quiet, compounding form of overspend that founders rarely put on a slide.

The trap is hiring a full-time CRO to do design work. You pay $350K-plus fully loaded for someone whose highest-value contribution — the playbook — is delivered in the first ninety days, after which they are an expensive operator supervising a team of three. That mismatch burns runway and often ends in a twelve-month parting when the board asks what the number is. Worse, the failure mode is self-concealing: the first two quarters look fine because the playbook work is genuinely valuable and the new hire is genuinely busy. The mismatch only surfaces later, when the design work is done, the team is still small, and the fully loaded cost keeps compounding against a number that has not yet inflected. By then you have spent both cash and the harder-to-recover currency of board confidence.

## When is the crossover point from fractional to full-time?

There is no revenue figure that automatically triggers a full-time hire, but a cluster of signals reliably marks the crossover. The clearest is **team size**: once you have four or more quota-carrying reps, someone needs to manage, coach, and forecast full-time, and a two-day-a-week leader cannot give that team the daily attention it needs. The second is **motion repeatability** — when the sales playbook is proven and the constraint has shifted from "figure out how to sell this" to "sell more of this, faster," you have moved from a design problem to a scaling problem. The third is **board and fundraising pressure**: if you are within two or three quarters of raising a Series B, having a permanent, accountable revenue owner who will still be there post-raise materially strengthens the story.

The decision tree below maps the common signals to a recommendation. Treat it as a starting diagnostic, not a verdict — most companies sit in a gray zone where a fractional-to-full-time bridge (discussed later) is the smartest path.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Series A revenue leadership gap] --> B{Is the sales motion repeatable}
    B -->|No still designing| C[Fractional CRO]
    B -->|Yes proven playbook| D{How many quota carrying reps}
    D -->|Three or fewer| E[Fractional CRO or VP Sales]
    D -->|Four or more| F{Series B within nine months}
    F -->|Yes| G[Full time CRO]
    F -->|No| H[Fractional CRO with scale mandate]
    C --> I[Reassess in two quarters]
    E --> I
    H --> I
```

Notice that the tree frequently routes to "reassess in two quarters." That is deliberate. The crossover is a moving target, and the cheapest way to find it is to start light and let the business tell you when the operating load has outgrown a part-time seat. Companies that commit to a full-time CRO before the motion is proven usually discover the mismatch the expensive way — through a failed hire and a reset.

A useful way to make the signals concrete is to watch three lagging-to-leading indicators over a rolling quarter. First, **the founder's calendar**: when the founder is spending more than a day or two a week inside individual deals and rep coaching, and that time is crowding out product and fundraising, the operating load has become continuous rather than episodic. Second, **onboarding throughput**: if you are hiring reps faster than a part-time leader can ramp them — meaning new hires sit for weeks without structured coaching or their time-to-first-deal is stretching — you have outgrown the fractional cadence. Third, **forecast frequency**: when the board or your own cash planning needs a defended forecast every single week rather than a quarterly review, someone has to own that rhythm as a full-time responsibility. Any one of these in isolation is noise; two or three together, sustained across a quarter, is the crossover announcing itself. The mistake is treating a single loud month — one big deal that wobbled, one heavy hiring sprint — as the signal, because the whole point of "reassess in two quarters" is to filter transient spikes from a durable shift in load.

It is also worth naming the anti-pattern: crossing over because of a *feeling* rather than a load. Founders frequently reach for a full-time CRO right after a board meeting where revenue was the uncomfortable topic, or right after a competitor announces a splashy executive hire. Neither is a load signal. If the underlying motion is still being designed, hiring a permanent operator to soothe board anxiety simply moves the discomfort forward a quarter and attaches a $350K price tag and a mis-hire risk to it. The crossover is earned by the state of the machine, not by the temperature of the last conversation about it.

## How do the economics compare on a fully loaded basis?

Founders anchor on base salary and dramatically underestimate the true cost of a full-time executive. A full-time CRO at a venture-backed Series A typically commands a base in the low-to-mid six figures, but the fully loaded figure — variable compensation tied to targets, benefits, payroll taxes, and, critically, **equity** — is far higher. A CRO-level equity grant at Series A commonly lands in the low single-digit percentage range, which is often the single most expensive line item over a multi-year horizon and the one founders discount most severely.

A fractional CRO, by contrast, is usually engaged on a monthly retainer for a defined commitment — often two to three days per week — with little or no equity and none of the employer overhead. The headline monthly number is real cash, but there is no benefits load, no severance exposure, and no cap-table dilution. Just as important is the **ramp and reversibility** difference: a fractional engagement can be scoped for a quarter and wound down cleanly, whereas a mis-hired full-time CRO carries recruiting cost, ramp time, opportunity cost, and often severance — a total that can approach a year of the role's cost with nothing to show for it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Total cost of revenue leadership] --> B[Full time CRO]
    A --> C[Fractional CRO]
    B --> D[Base salary]
    B --> E[Variable comp]
    B --> F[Benefits and taxes]
    B --> G[Equity grant]
    B --> H[Mis hire risk severance]
    C --> I[Monthly retainer]
    C --> J[No equity typical]
    C --> K[No employer overhead]
    C --> L[Wind down clean]
```

The honest framing is not "fractional is cheaper" — it is that fractional converts a large fixed, hard-to-reverse commitment into a smaller variable, easy-to-reverse one at exactly the stage when your certainty about what you need is lowest. That optionality has real value on a Series A balance sheet where every month of runway is contested. For a structured way to model the burn tradeoff against pipeline output, the [pipeline efficiency and burn guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-pipeline-burn) walks through the unit-economics math.

There is a second economic lens that founders almost never apply: the cost of the decision itself, expressed in runway-months. At Series A, the scarcest currency is not dollars but *time to prove the next milestone*. Every fixed executive commitment you take on shortens the runway over which you get to learn before you must raise again. A fractional engagement keeps that learning window open — you spend a smaller, controllable amount to discover what the full-time role should actually be, and you preserve the ability to redirect that spend if the business teaches you something new. A premature full-time hire does the opposite: it front-loads your largest people cost against your least-certain understanding of the role, and if it fails, the six-to-nine-month recovery is subtracted directly from the runway you were counting on to reach Series B. In other words, the fractional model is not just cheaper on the spreadsheet in a given month — it is *cheaper in optionality*, which at this stage is the more expensive resource to lose.

It is worth stating the case *for* the full-time cost too, so the comparison is honest. When the motion is genuinely proven and the operating load is genuinely continuous, the full-time premium buys things a retainer cannot: total attention, deeper accountability, the ability to attract senior reps who want to work for a permanent leader, and an equity-aligned owner whose upside is your upside. The equity that looks like the scariest line item on a cap-table model is, past the crossover, the mechanism that binds a great operator to a multi-year outcome. The point is not that full-time is overpriced — it is that it is correctly priced for a stage you have to earn your way into, and paying that price early means paying for alignment and attention you cannot yet fully use.

## What are the real risks of each model?

The fractional model's central risk is **shallow ownership**. A part-time leader splits attention across multiple clients, is not in every internal conversation, and cannot absorb the ambient context a full-timer accumulates. When a key deal wobbles on a Thursday, the fractional CRO may not hear about it until the Monday sync. This is mitigated by tight scoping, weekly cadence, and — importantly — a strong internal operator (a sales manager or head of RevOps) who owns day-to-day execution while the fractional leader owns strategy. Fractional works best as *architecture plus coaching*, not as *daily firefighting*.

The full-time model's central risk is **premature commitment to the wrong person or the wrong stage**. Hiring a full-time CRO before the motion is proven asks a scaling specialist to do design work they may not be suited for, or asks a builder to sign up for a role that will soon need a different skill set. Executive mis-hires at this level are among the costliest mistakes a Series A company makes, both in direct cost and in the six-to-nine months of lost momentum while the team churns. There is also a subtler risk: a full-time CRO changes the org's center of gravity. The founder often steps back from revenue at precisely the moment their product intuition is still the company's sharpest selling tool, and an early full-time hire can accelerate that handoff before the company is ready for it.

A second-order risk on both sides is **misaligned scope**. Whether fractional or full-time, if the mandate is vague — "own revenue" with no agreement on which of sales, marketing, CS, and RevOps actually report in — the leader inherits accountability without authority. Clarify the surface area before you sign anyone, and revisit it as the org grows.

A third risk, specific to the fractional model, is **institutional-knowledge leakage**. A part-time leader who is doing genuinely strategic work carries a lot of the "why" in their head — why the ICP was narrowed, why a channel was killed, why the comp plan is shaped the way it is. If that context lives only with someone who is contractually temporary, a clean wind-down can accidentally strip the company of its own reasoning. The mitigation is procedural, not personal: insist that the fractional leader documents decisions and playbooks *into the company's own systems* as they go, not into their private deck library, so that the artifacts survive the engagement even if the person does not. A fractional CRO who leaves behind a written, owned, versioned playbook has de-risked their own departure; one who leaves behind only a Slack history has quietly recreated the single-point-of-failure they were hired to remove.

And there is a symmetrical, quieter risk on the full-time side worth naming: **over-hiring the title to under-hire the work**. Some founders, anxious about looking under-built to investors, hire a full-time CRO as a signaling move and then fail to give the role the authority, budget, or team that justifies the seat. The result is an expensive executive with a two-person org and no levers — a person set up to fail by the very insecurity that hired them. If you would not give the role real authority over marketing, CS, and RevOps within a year, you are hiring a VP of Sales with an inflated title, and both the cap table and the eventual working relationship will pay for the mismatch.

## How should a founder structure the engagement to de-risk the decision?

The strongest play for most Series A companies is a **fractional-to-full-time bridge**. Engage a fractional CRO with an explicit dual mandate: (1) design and instrument the revenue engine now, and (2) define the hiring profile — and ideally help recruit — the eventual full-time leader. This turns the fractional engagement into a diligence exercise. By the time you are ready for a full-timer, you have a proven playbook, clean metrics, a scorecard for the role, and a leader who has already stress-tested what "good" looks like in your specific motion. The bridge structure also lets you discover the crossover point empirically rather than guessing it.

Whichever model you choose, insist on a few non-negotiables. Define the **surface area** in writing (which functions report in). Set **90-day and 180-day outcomes** that are measurable — pipeline coverage, ramp time to first closed deal for new reps, forecast accuracy — not vague "build the team" goals. Establish a **weekly operating cadence** so a part-time leader still has a real pulse on the business. And build an **off-ramp** on both sides: a clean wind-down clause for fractional, a defined ramp-and-review checkpoint for full-time. The goal is to make the decision reversible cheaply, because at Series A your information about what you need is still improving month over month. Founders who want a template for scoping revenue-leadership outcomes can start from the [revenue leadership scorecard](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/qa-revenue-leader-scorecard) and adapt it to their stage.

A practical way to sequence the bridge is to run it in three explicit phases with named exits. **Phase one (roughly the first sixty to ninety days) is diagnosis and design**: the fractional leader audits the funnel, rewrites the ICP and playbook, cleans up the CRM and reporting, and produces a written revenue model. The exit criterion is a documented, agreed-upon motion — not a revenue number, which is too lagging to react to. **Phase two is proof**: the fractional leader hires or re-coaches the first cohort of real closers and runs the playbook long enough to show it is repeatable across more than one rep and more than one deal type. The exit criterion here is repeatability evidence — two or more reps hitting ramp on the same motion — because a single rep's success can be talent, not system. **Phase three is handoff design**: with a proven motion in hand, the fractional leader writes the scorecard for the permanent hire, helps interview candidates against it, and defines the first ninety days of the full-timer's onboarding. Structuring the engagement this way means each phase produces an artifact the company keeps, and each exit is a real decision point where you can extend, wind down, or convert to full-time with actual evidence rather than a hunch.

Finally, protect the founder's role deliberately during all of this. The most common way the bridge goes wrong is that the founder, relieved to have senior help, disengages from revenue entirely and treats the fractional leader as a replacement rather than a force multiplier. At Series A that is premature: the founder's product intuition and customer relationships are still the sharpest instruments the company owns, and the fractional model works precisely because it augments them rather than supplanting them. The right posture is a genuine partnership — the fractional leader builds the system and coaches the team, while the founder stays close enough to the market to keep the strategy honest. Handing off the last mile of founder-led selling is a milestone for the *full-time* era, earned once the machine is proven, not a convenience to be claimed the day the fractional contract is signed.

## Related questions

### Is a VP of Sales a better first hire than a CRO at Series A?

Often, yes. If your gap is purely front-line selling and rep management — not marketing, CS, and RevOps orchestration — a VP of Sales is a more focused, less expensive hire. Reserve the CRO title for when you genuinely need cross-functional revenue ownership.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO typically work?

Most engagements land at two to three days per week, scoped to a monthly retainer. Some start heavier during the initial diagnostic and playbook-build phase, then taper to a lighter coaching cadence once the operators are running the system.

### Can a founder be their own CRO at Series A?

For a while, yes — many founders should keep owning revenue through early Series A because their product intuition is the sharpest sales tool the company has. The signal to bring in help is when revenue leadership consistently crowds out product and fundraising work.

### What equity does a full-time CRO expect at Series A?

Grants commonly fall in the low single-digit percentage range, vesting over four years, and this is usually the largest true cost of the hire. Fractional CROs typically take little to no equity, trading upside for flexibility and cash.

### Does a fractional CRO help you raise a Series B?

Indirectly and meaningfully. They instrument the metrics a Series B lead will diligence and prove the motion is repeatable. Some structure the engagement specifically to hand a clean, defensible revenue story to the eventual full-time leader before the raise.

## FAQ

**What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a consultant?**
A fractional CRO holds real operating accountability — they own revenue outcomes, manage the team, and sit in leadership meetings — whereas a consultant advises and hands off recommendations. Fractional is embedded leadership on a part-time basis; consulting is external advice.

**At what ARR should a Series A company hire a full-time CRO?**
There is no fixed threshold, but many companies cross over in the mid-single-digit millions of ARR, once the motion is repeatable and there are four or more reps to manage. Team size and repeatability are better triggers than ARR alone.

**Can a fractional CRO become the full-time CRO later?**
Sometimes, and it can be an ideal path if the fit is strong and the person wants the full-time seat. More often the fractional leader is a specialist in the build phase who helps recruit a different profile for the scale phase. Agree upfront on which outcome you are aiming for.

**How long do fractional CRO engagements usually last?**
Commonly six to twelve months, long enough to design the engine, hire the first real closers, and prove repeatability. Some extend into ongoing lighter-touch coaching; others wind down cleanly once a full-time leader is in place.

**Will investors object to a fractional CRO?**
Generally no, and many investors actively prefer it at Series A because it conserves runway and avoids a premature executive commitment. What investors dislike is *no* revenue leadership and *no* metrics — not a part-time leader who has instrumented the business well.

**What happens to the sales team's morale with a part-time leader?**
It depends entirely on internal ownership. If a strong internal operator runs day-to-day execution while the fractional CRO owns strategy and coaching, morale holds. Problems arise when the team has no daily leader and the fractional CRO is treated as a firefighter.

**Should marketing report to the CRO at Series A?**
Not always. Many Series A companies keep demand generation reporting to the founder or a separate marketing lead and scope the CRO to sales and RevOps. Define the reporting surface explicitly rather than assuming the title implies all of revenue.

**How do I measure whether a fractional CRO is working?**
Track leading indicators tied to their mandate: pipeline coverage ratio, new-rep ramp time to first closed deal, forecast accuracy, and playbook adoption. These show whether the engine is being built, well before the lagging revenue number moves.

**What red flags suggest a fractional CRO is the wrong fit?**
Watch for a leader who resists documenting playbooks into your systems, who is spread across too many clients to keep the weekly cadence, or who defaults to firefighting individual deals instead of building the motion. A fractional CRO who cannot point to owned, transferable artifacts by day ninety is functioning as an expensive contractor, not a systems builder.

**How do I transition from a fractional to a full-time CRO without disruption?**
Treat the handoff as a designed phase, not an event. Have the fractional leader write the role scorecard, help interview against it, and stay on in a lighter advisory capacity through the full-timer's first sixty to ninety days. The overlap protects institutional knowledge and gives the permanent hire a running start instead of a cold reset.
